analysis.one_liner: Bars banks from selling their own or affiliates' investments at deposit-taking counters to protect depositors.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 51 cosponsors and two days of subcommittee hearings, never got a vote in the House Banking Committee and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1990, banks were increasingly selling stocks, bonds, mutual funds, and other investments right at the teller counter where customers make deposits. This bill would prohibit insured banks from selling investments in themselves or their affiliates in the public areas of deposit-taking branches, and would let federal banking regulators ban or restrict other sales that customers are likely to confuse with government-insured deposits. The concern is that a customer could buy a risky investment thinking it is as safe as an FDIC-insured savings account. The bill was introduced by Rep. Charles Schumer with 51 cosponsors from both parties, got referred to the House Banking Committee and its financial institutions subcommittee, and two days of hearings were held in March 1990. It was never reported to the full House and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary bank customers, especially less sophisticated savers and older depositors, who would be protected from buying un insured investments at the deposit counter believing they carry federal deposit insurance. Federal bank regulators would gain clearer authority to restrict confusing sales.

how_it_helps.text: Banks would be barred from selling stocks, bonds, or other ownership interests in their own affiliates in any office space open to the public for accepting deposits, removing the risk that customers buy them at the teller counter thinking they are insured deposits.

Banks would also be barred from selling their own debt or stock where the proceeds count toward the bank's required capital, a practice that can shore up a bank's finances using customer funds raised at the deposit window.

Federal banking agencies could prohibit or set conditions on other sales of a bank's or affiliate's securities in public deposit areas if they determine customers are likely to confuse the products with insured deposits.
Everyday payment instruments like deposits, traveler's checks, cashier's checks, certified checks, and money orders would be expressly exempted, so routine banking would be unaffected.

analysis.who_pays: Insured banks and their securities affiliates, which would lose the ability to market their own and their affiliates' investment products at the teller counter, one of the most convenient retail channels to reach millions of depositors.

drawbacks.text: The ban is location-based: banks could still sell affiliate securities elsewhere, so the bill limits one sales channel rather than banning the products, but banks lose a low-cost way to reach customers, and bank-affiliated securities underwriting, a growing business in 1990, would face a constraint on its most visible storefront.

Requiring regulators to judge when a product is 'likely to be confused' with an insured deposit invites judgment calls and could lead to rules that block products some customers actually want to buy from their own bank.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protection is targeted and narrow: it does not ban banks from selling investments, only from doing it in the place designed for accepting federally insured deposits, and it keeps regulators in charge of borderline cases. The cost falls on banks' marketing convenience, not on any customer's access to products, which remain available elsewhere. The main honest objection is that a counter-area ban is easier for banks to route around than a rule about how products are disclosed, and that confusing sales could simply move to the desk ten feet away.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking Committee and then to its financial institutions subcommittee, which held hearings in March 1990, but the committee never reported it to the House and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Schumer of New York, joined by Rep. McMillen of Maryland, introduced the Depositor Protection and Fraud Act of 1990 on February 21, 1990.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs, and on March 1 to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions Supervision, Regulation and Insurance.
The subcommittee held hearings on March 14 and 15, 1990.
The bill attracted 51 cosponsors, 49 Democrats and 2 Republicans.
The committee never reported the bill to the House, no floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and their securities affiliates kept the ability to sell their own and affiliates' investment products at the deposit counter, and depositors got no added protection against confusing those products with insured deposits.

for.name: Charles E. Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured 51 cosponsors; the subcommittee he referred it to held two days of hearings.

for.name: Thomas McMillen
for.what_they_did: Joined Schumer as the bill's other original sponsor.

against.name: Henry B. Gonzalez
against.role: Chair, House Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee referred the bill to a subcommittee, held hearings, and never reported it to the full House, keeping it from a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship crossed party lines, 49 Democrats and 2 Republicans, and the record shows no organized floor opposition because the bill never left committee; the deciding event was the Banking Committee's failure to act.

industries.note: The bill would bar banks from selling their own or affiliates' securities at the deposit counter, closing a convenient retail channel for bank-affiliated underwriting that was expanding in 1990. Banks' interest in keeping that channel ran against depositors' interest in not mistaking un insured investments for insured deposits.

industries.industry: Federal banking regulators (FDIC, OCC, Federal Reserve)
industries.note: The bill would give agencies explicit authority to prohibit or condition sales of securities likely to be confused with insured deposits, adding a consumer-protection tool.
